summary: This unit helps a Level 3 welder plan the move to running a fabrication business. You will audit your skills, do a personal SWOT and set dated goals, find and test a niche, cost and price jobs, work out break-even and cash flow, choose finance, set the business up legally and safely in Jamaica, win and keep customers, and review the strategy as you go.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It helps you work out a **personal entrepreneurial strategy**: a realistic, dated plan for moving from working for someone else to running your own fabrication business. You will look honestly at your own skills and situation, find a part of the market you can serve well, cost and price jobs, plan the money, set the business up legally and safely, win and keep customers, and review the plan as you go.

Many Jamaican welders dream of their own shop, and many succeed. Others fail, often not because their welding is poor, but because they priced jobs wrongly, ran out of cash while waiting to be paid, or started before they were ready. A good strategy turns the dream into steps, each with a date, so you can see whether you are on track.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and any skilled tradesperson thinking about working for themselves. The examples come from fabrication, but the methods suit any trade.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means for you
rows: Write a clear, dated long-term goal and the yearly milestones that lead to it.
Carry out an honest skills audit and a personal SWOT analysis, and use them to shape the plan.
Spot a real opportunity that matches your skills, and test it with market research.
Work out direct costs and overheads, add profit, set a charge-out rate, and find the break-even point.
Work out start-up costs, choose how to pay for them, and forecast cash flow.
Choose a business structure, register, meet tax duties, insure, and meet your duties as an employer.
Choose your customers and selling point, market the business, write clear quotations and give good service.
Control the main risks, decide when and how to grow, and use advice and support.
Check progress against goals at set times, and change the plan when needed.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on goals, self-assessment, niches, market research, registration, insurance, costing, pricing, break-even, cash flow, finance, the business plan, marketing, quotations, tax, risk, growth, support and review.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms and sums) and essays, for example a four-year strategy, a personal SWOT, choosing a niche, pricing a staircase, break-even, legal set-up, financing equipment, risks, marketing and reviewing the strategy.

**Two group practicals**: a personal skills audit and SWOT, a niche tested by a short survey, and a four-year strategy poster; and a costed quotation, break-even, 12-month cash flow forecast and business plan summary presented at a role-played loan meeting.

blocks.note: Practise the sums: direct cost, mark-up, margin, charge-out rate, break-even, loan interest and cash flow balances. Write each step down and check it a second way. GCT is always added "at the current rate".
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Being an entrepreneur and your personal strategy

blocks.p: An **entrepreneur** is someone who spots an opportunity, takes the risk of starting a business to meet it, and organises the money, people and work to make it pay. Being self-employed brings freedom and the chance to earn more, but also uncertain income, long hours, and responsibility for everything: sales, books, tax, safety and staff.

head: Working for a shop
Running your own shop
rows: Regular wage, paid whether work is busy or slow
Income depends on sales, prices and getting paid
The employer provides machines, premises and insurance
You buy, maintain and insure them
You find, price, win and keep the customers
You handle your own tax and contributions, and your workers'
Often long hours, especially at first

blocks.h: Routes into business for a welder

ul: **Weekend and evening jobs** while still employed, to build skills, customers and savings with little risk.
**A mobile service** (repairs on site from a van or pickup), with low start-up costs.
**Subcontracting** to builders and larger fabricators.
**Your own shop**, alone or with a helper, then growing.
**A partnership** with someone whose skills complement yours, for example a welder and a salesperson or bookkeeper.

blocks.h: What a personal entrepreneurial strategy contains

head: Part
What it says
rows: Where you want to be, by when, written so you will know when you have got there
Your skills audit, your personal SWOT, your savings and commitments
Who your customers will be, what you will offer, and why they will choose you
Yearly (or six-monthly) steps: skills, savings, registration, equipment, premises, first hire
Start-up costs, how you will pay for them, prices, break-even and cash flow
What could go wrong, and how you will control it
When and how you will check progress and change the plan

blocks.note: Your family is part of the plan. Talk with them about the savings needed, the risk, the hours and the income in the first year, and agree what you will do if the business is slow to start.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Knowing yourself: skills audit, SWOT and goals

blocks.p: A **skills audit** lists the skills a business owner needs and rates honestly how good you are at each, so you can see what you still lack and plan how to get it.

head: Skill area
Examples
How to fill a gap
rows: Welding processes and positions, stainless and aluminium, reading drawings, site installation
Courses and qualification tests through HEART/NSTA Trust or other providers; practice
Pricing and estimating, bookkeeping, cash flow, tax, contracts
Short business courses; advice from the JBDC; a mentor; an accountant
Talking to clients, writing quotations, handling complaints
Practice; a mentor; watching a good salesperson
Self-discipline, time management, coping with stress, leading staff
Planning tools; support from family and mentor
Save, plan and get them in order

blocks.p: A **SWOT** analysis looks at your **Strengths** and **Weaknesses** (inside you: skills, money, contacts) and the **Opportunities** and **Threats** around you (outside: the market, rivals, prices, the economy).

head: Strengths (inside, helpful)
Weaknesses (inside, harmful)
rows: A reputation for neat, reliable work
Little experience of pricing or bookkeeping

head: Opportunities (outside, helpful)
Threats (outside, harmful)
rows: Hotels and villas needing railings and repairs
Rising steel prices and exchange rate
Customers who pay late, or not at all

blocks.p: The SWOT is only useful if it shapes the strategy:

ul: **Use strengths to take opportunities**: builder contacts and neat work to win grille and gate work on the new housing schemes.
**Fix weaknesses**: a bookkeeping course and a mentor; save before leaving the job; get the licence.
**Use strengths to reduce threats**: offer made-to-measure, galvanised work that imported grilles cannot match.
**Avoid the worst combinations**: do not take big jobs on long credit while savings are small; ask for deposits.

blocks.p: Your main goal should be **specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART)**. "Run a three-person gate and grille shop in May Pen by 2030" can be checked; "be my own boss some day" cannot. Each step towards it needs a date, so progress can be checked and kept on track.

head: Year
Example milestones
rows: Keep the job; gain a stainless steel TIG qualification; finish a bookkeeping course; save J$30,000 a month in a separate account; get a driver's licence
Register a business name; do weekend jobs to build a customer list; keep job cards and photos of every job; study the market and choose a niche
Write a business plan with a cash flow forecast; buy the main tools; find premises; meet a mentor and a lender
Leave the job; open the shop; hire a helper once work is steady; review the plan every three months

blocks.p: Build up an **emergency fund** before you leave a paid job, to live on while the business is slow at first. A common aim is several months of household costs. If the household needs J$120,000 a month and you want six months' cover, that is 6 × 120,000 = **J$720,000**, kept apart from the money for the business.

sections.title: Finding a niche and testing it

blocks.p: A **niche** is a small, special part of the market that a business chooses to serve, and serves better than others. A new business that does what every other shop does must compete on price; one that specialises can face fewer rivals and charge fairly for its skill.

head: Possible niche
Who buys
What it needs from you
rows: Security grilles and gates for new homes
Neat, made-to-measure work; fast fitting; galvanising
Hotels, villas, restaurants on the coast
TIG on stainless, polishing, careful site work
Pipe qualifications, site safety systems, quick response
Heavy repairs, MIG, a yard with space

ul: Customers are **waiting** for the work or travelling far for it: builders in the area wait weeks for steel stairs.
There are **few good rivals**, or the rivals are slow, unreliable or far away.
Customers will **pay a fair price** for quality or speed.
The work matches **your skills**, or skills you can get.
The demand is **steady**, not a one-off.

blocks.p: Market research tests the idea **before** you spend money on it.

head: Method
What you learn
rows: How many there are, what they make, their prices, how long customers wait
Talk to possible customers: builders, hotel maintenance managers, farmers, hardware stores
What they buy, how often, what they pay now, what problems they have
Answers from a fair number of possible customers
Whether people will actually pay, and what the work really costs
New housing schemes, hotels and factories planned in the area

ul: Ask people who would really buy, not just family and friends who want to be kind.
Ask about facts (what they buy now, how often, what they pay, how long they wait), not just "would you use my service?".
Ask enough people, and write the answers down.
If the results show steady demand at fair prices, go ahead; if not, change the idea.

blocks.p: A **unique selling point (USP)** is the promise that makes customers choose you over your rivals, and that they can check. "Galvanised gates, fitted within ten days" is a clear promise; "best quality" is what everyone says.

head: Kind of cost
What it is
Fabrication examples
rows: The steel and rods used on that gate; labour hours on that job; galvanising for that job
Costs of running the business, whatever jobs are done
Rent, electricity, phone, insurance, vehicle, accountant, loan repayments
Stay the same each month however much work is done
Rent, insurance, the owner's basic wage, loan repayments
Rise and fall with the amount of work

flow: List the materials from the drawing and price them
Add consumables: rods or wire, gas, discs, primer
Work out the labour: hours × the hourly rate
Add them up: the direct cost
Add a share of the overheads
Add profit (and a small contingency for risk)
If the business is registered for GCT, add GCT at the current rate
Check the price against what rivals charge and what the customer will pay

head: Line
Worked example: a set of security grilles
rows: Added at the current rate, only if the business is registered

blocks.p: **Mark-up** is profit as a percentage of **cost**. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the **selling price**. A gate costing J$80,000 and sold for J$100,000 makes J$20,000: a mark-up of 20,000 ÷ 80,000 = 25%, but a margin of 20,000 ÷ 100,000 = 20%. Know which one you mean.
Adding percentages one after the other is not the same as adding them together: 20% then 10% on J$100,000 gives 100,000 × 1.2 × 1.1 = J$132,000, not J$130,000.

The **charge-out rate** is the lowest hourly rate that covers your wage and your overheads. **Charge-out rate = (wage you need for the year + yearly overheads) ÷ chargeable hours in the year.** Chargeable hours are only the hours you can bill to customers, not the hours spent quoting, buying, travelling and doing the books.

The **break-even point** is the level of sales at which income just equals all the costs: no profit, no loss. For each job, the **contribution** is the price minus its variable costs: what is left towards the fixed costs. **Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per job.**

Example: fixed costs are J$270,000 a month, and each gate leaves J$30,000 after its steel, consumables and labour. Break-even = 270,000 ÷ 30,000 = **9 gates a month**. The 10th gate onwards makes a profit. The owner can use this to set sales targets, check that prices are high enough, see the effect of a rent rise or a new machine, and test whether the idea is realistic before starting.

Every job gets a **job card** recording the hours and materials actually used. Comparing the real cost with the quote shows which jobs make money and which do not, and makes the next quote more accurate.

sections.title: Money: start-up funding and cash flow

ul: Equipment: welding sets, cutting equipment, grinders, drills, clamps, benches, PPE.
Vehicle, or the cost of hiring transport.
Premises: deposit and rent, electrical work (many machines need 220 V and enough supply), security.
Registration, insurance, signs, a phone, business cards.
Opening stock of steel and consumables.
**Working capital**: cash to pay for materials and wages until customers pay.

head: Source
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: No interest, no debt; you keep full control
Takes time to build; less left for emergencies
Can strain relationships; agree terms in writing
Loan from a bank or credit union
A large sum at once; you keep full ownership
Repaid with interest every month, even when work is slow; may need security (collateral)
Use the machine now; spread the cost; you own it at the end
Total cost usually higher; it can be taken back if you miss payments
Low payments; servicing may be included
You may never own it; total cost higher
Money and maybe skills without a loan
No large outlay for equipment used rarely
Cost each time; less control over timing

blocks.p: Many owners mix these: savings for tools and the deposit, a loan or hire purchase for the large machines. A machine needed for about one job a year is usually hired, or the work subcontracted, rather than bought. Some loans for small businesses are funded through the Development Bank of Jamaica and offered through banks and credit unions; ask lenders what is available.

**Collateral** (security) is something of value, such as a vehicle or a land title, that the lender may take if the loan is not repaid. **Interest** is the cost of borrowing: a J$500,000 loan repaid as 24 payments of J$25,000 costs 24 × 25,000 = J$600,000, so the interest is **J$100,000**.

**Cash flow** is the timing of money coming in and going out. A profitable business can still fail if it runs out of cash, for example on a large job where steel and wages are paid months before the client pays. A **cash flow forecast** is a month-by-month table of expected cash in and cash out. Lenders ask to see it, because it shows when a loan could be repaid.

head: Cash flow
Month 1 (J$)
Month 2 (J$)
Month 3 (J$)
rows: Cash out: wages, rent and other costs

blocks.p: Each month: closing balance = opening balance + cash in − cash out, and the closing balance becomes the next month's opening balance. Here the business needs about J$90,000 of extra finance (an overdraft or a deposit from a client) arranged **before** month 1.

ul: Take a **deposit** large enough to buy the materials, then **stage payments** (for example after fabrication and after fitting), and the balance on completion.
Invoice promptly, and follow up overdue accounts. **Debtors** are customers who owe you money; **creditors** are suppliers you owe.
Keep the business's money in its own bank account, separate from household money.
Do not buy more stock than the next jobs need.
Arrange an overdraft or loan before you need it, not when you are already short.

head: Structure
What it means
Points to know
rows: You own and run the business yourself
Simple and cheap to set up; you keep all the profit; but you are personally liable for all its debts
Two or more people own it together
Share skills, money and work; each partner can be liable for the business's debts; write a partnership agreement
A separate legal body owned by its shareholders and run by its directors
Owners' liability is limited, so their homes are not normally at risk for business debts; more paperwork and yearly filings; lenders may still ask directors for personal guarantees

flow: Choose a business name, and check it is not already in use
Register the business name, or form the company, with the Companies Office of Jamaica (the registration form can also register you with the tax and statutory bodies; check the current forms)
Have a taxpayer registration number (TRN), and register the business with Tax Administration Jamaica
Keep proper records and file income tax returns on time; as a self-employed person you are also responsible for your own statutory contributions
Register for GCT once sales pass the set level, and then charge GCT at the current rate. Only a registered business may charge GCT
Keep a tax compliance certificate (TCC) up to date if you want to bid for government contracts

blocks.p: Check with the municipal corporation (formerly the municipal corporation) that your premises may be used for fabrication: noise, fumes, sparks and deliveries can be a problem in a residential area. Check the electrical supply, and have any electrical work done by a qualified electrician.

head: Insurance
What it covers
rows: Your machines, tools and stock against fire, theft and storm damage
Harm the business causes to members of the public or their property, for example a spark starting a fire at a customer's house
Your van or pickup (required by law)
Lost income while you cannot work, for example after a hurricane

ul: Give written terms of employment: pay, hours, duties, leave.
Register as an employer, make the statutory payroll deductions (income tax, NIS, NHT and education tax) and the employer's contributions, and pay them over on time.
Provide a safe workplace, safe machines, the right PPE, training and supervision.
Follow employment law on hours, overtime, holidays with pay and fair treatment.

blocks.note: One serious injury can close a small shop: lost work, claims, higher insurance, and a damaged name. Safety is not extra cost; it protects the business.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Build to the drawing. If a builder asks for thinner tube than the drawing shows to save money, refuse unless the engineer approves the change in writing.
Give a proper receipt for every sale and record it, even when a customer offers cash "with no receipt".
Use photos of customers' jobs only with their agreement.

blocks.p: Decide who your main customers are (builders, home owners, hotels, farmers, factories), what they care about most (price, speed, quality, reliability), and where they can be reached. Then make your selling point match what they value.

head: Marketing method
Points to know
rows: Keep a phone album, a printed folder and social-media posts, with each customer's agreement. Photos show quality better than words
Take photos and business cards; builders give repeat work
Leave cards; they are asked for recommendations
Your name and number on the van and on a small plate on finished work
Ask happy customers to tell others; the best and cheapest marketing
Quick replies, clear photos, prices on request; answer messages promptly

blocks.p: A **quotation** is a written offer to do a job for a stated price. A clear quotation prevents disputes.

ul: What is **included**: the items, sizes, materials, finish (for example galvanised or primed), delivery and fitting.
What is **left out**: for example painting, concrete work, electrical work or making good walls.
The **price**, with GCT shown at the current rate if you are registered.
The **payment terms**: deposit, stage payments, balance on completion.
How long the price is **valid**, and the expected time to finish.
Your business name, contact details and the date.

blocks.p: If the client asks for extra work during the job, agree the extra price **in writing** first. This written change to the contract is called a **variation**. Without it, the extra work may never be paid for.

ul: Do what you promised: good welding, accurate fitting, on time, and a clean site.
Keep the customer informed, especially about delays.
Fix problems quickly and politely, without arguing.
Follow up after the job; ask for feedback and referrals.
**Repeat orders and referrals** are the best sign that customers are happy.

blocks.h: The main risks and their controls

head: Risk
How the owner controls it
rows: Safety: burns, eye injuries, falls, fire
Safe machines, PPE, training, extinguishers, insurance
Cash flow: running short while waiting to be paid
Cash flow forecast, deposits and stage payments, a cash reserve, an overdraft arranged early
Quality: a poor weld or a gate that does not fit
Work to drawings, check before delivery, train staff
Steel prices: a rise wipes out the profit on a quoted job
Short validity on quotes, buy steel when the job is confirmed, a small contingency
Bad debts: a customer never pays
Check new customers, written agreements, deposits, prompt invoices, follow-up
Insurance, a storm plan, secure premises, a generator or planned working
Reasonable hours, rest, a backup plan for illness

blocks.p: Review the strategy at set times, for example **every three months**, and also when something big changes, such as losing a major customer or a steep rise in steel prices. Compare what has happened with the goals and dates, find the reason for any gap, and change the plan, writing down new dates.

head: Measure
What it shows
rows: Whether enough work is coming in
Profit on each job against its quote
Whether pricing is right; which kinds of job pay
Cash in the bank, and money owed to you
Whether the work is well planned
Whether your personal goals are on track

blocks.p: If records show that one kind of job loses money, find out why (pricing, wasted material, slow methods), then reprice it, improve it or stop doing it.

ul: Before hiring when you are turning work away, check your cash flow: can you pay a wage every week, even in a slow month?
Subcontract specialist work, such as galvanising, when your volume would never pay for the equipment.
Train and qualify before you quote for a new kind of work, such as stainless steel.
Grow in steps, and review after each one.

head: Support
How it helps
rows: An experienced business person to talk big decisions through with, especially in the first year
Advice, training and support for small businesses
HEART/NSTA Trust and other training providers
Technical and business skills and qualifications
Contacts, training, shared advice, a voice for small firms
Books, tax returns, advice on structure and GCT
Accounts, loans, overdrafts, advice on what lenders need

blocks.note: A one-person shop working 80-hour weeks for months risks tired mistakes, accidents and poor health, and then the business stops. Plan rest, as you plan work.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a personal entrepreneurial strategy is and what it contains.
I can compare being employed with running my own business.
I can carry out an honest skills audit and plan how to fill the gaps.
I can complete a personal SWOT and use it to shape my strategy.
I can write a SMART main goal with dated yearly milestones.
I can work out the emergency fund I need before leaving a paid job.
I can choose a niche and test it with market research.
I can write a clear unique selling point.
I can tell direct costs from overheads, and fixed costs from variable costs.
I can build up a price with overheads, profit and GCT at the current rate.
I can tell mark-up from margin, and work out a charge-out rate.
I can work out a break-even point and use it to make decisions.
I can list start-up costs and compare ways of paying for them.
I can work out loan interest and build a simple cash flow forecast.
I can explain the business structures and the steps to set up legally in Jamaica.
I can name the insurance a fabrication shop needs and my duties as an employer.
I can write a clear quotation and handle a variation.

The timing of money coming into and going out of a business

c1.title: A welder's plan in Ewarton
c1.text: Chevaughn, 29, is a Level 3 welder with a maintenance contractor in Ewarton, St Catherine. He wants his own fabrication shop within four years. His skills audit shows strong MMAW, MIG and 6G pipe skills, but no experience of pricing, bookkeeping or selling, and he has no driver's licence. Several agro-processing plants nearby need pipework repairs, and new housing schemes are being built in the area. He has J$350,000 saved, and his household costs J$120,000 a month.

c2.title: Pricing a staircase in Balaclava
c2.text: Kadeem runs a small fabrication shop in Balaclava, St Elizabeth, and is pricing a steel staircase for Mrs Ebanks. Materials will cost J$150,000; consumables (rods, discs, gas and primer) J$20,000; and labour 50 hours at J$1,600 an hour. The shop adds 20% to the direct cost for overheads, then 10% for profit. Kadeem's sales are below the level at which a business must register for GCT, and he has not registered.

c3.title: A hotel contract in Runaway Bay
c3.text: Garfield's shop in Runaway Bay, St Ann, has won a J$2.4 million contract for balcony railings for a hotel's new block. The hotel will pay 60 days after each invoice. Steel and galvanising, J$1.1 million, must be paid for in the first month, and wages are J$300,000 a month. Garfield has J$500,000 in the bank. He also needs a new MIG set costing J$450,000.

c4.title: Looking for a niche in Whitehouse
c4.text: Trudy-Ann, a Level 3 welder in Whitehouse, Westmoreland, holds a TIG qualification on stainless steel and wants to start her own business. Three general welding shops within 10 km make gates and grilles. She asked 12 hotel and villa maintenance managers along the coast about stainless steel railings and fittings: 9 said they send repairs to Kingston and wait 4 to 6 weeks for them.

c5.title: A two-year review in Spaldings
c5.text: Orville has run a fabrication shop in Spaldings, Clarendon, for two years. His strategy said he would hire his first helper by month 18; it is now month 24 and he has not. His job records for the last six months show an average profit of J$6,000 on each of 18 gates and J$18,000 on each of 10 water-tank stands. His fixed costs are J$192,000 a month, and each tank stand leaves J$24,000 towards them after its steel, consumables and labour.

questions.q: Which is the best first-year milestone for Chevaughn?
o: Open his own shop and hire two helpers within the first year
Become a much better businessman over the next twelve months
Do a bookkeeping course and save J$30,000 a month this year
Save as much money as he possibly can during the first year
questions.why: It tackles a weakness from his skills audit and builds savings, and both parts are measurable and dated. Opening a shop in year one skips the preparation; the others cannot be checked.

questions.q: His SWOT shows strong pipe skills and nearby plants that need pipework. What does this suggest?
o: Burglar bars for the new homes, the work most shops already do
Small welding repairs for anyone who happens to walk in
Selling imported ready-made gates from a roadside stall
Pipework repairs and maintenance for the nearby plants
questions.why: Matching a strength (6G pipe skills) to an opportunity (plants needing pipework) points to a niche with fewer rivals, where his skill is worth paying for.

questions.q: Chevaughn wants six months of household costs saved before he leaves his job. How much is that?
questions.why: 6 × J$120,000 = J$720,000, kept apart from the business money. His J$350,000 covers less than three months.

questions.q: Which step would best deal with his weakness in pricing and keeping books?
o: Let each customer suggest a price for the job
Copy the prices of the cheapest shop in the area
Do a short bookkeeping course and find a mentor
Leave the books until the shop is making money
questions.why: A course gives him the skills and a mentor helps him apply them. Copying the cheapest rival or letting customers set prices ignores his own costs, and neglected books hide losses.

questions.q: What is the direct cost of the staircase?
questions.why: Labour is 50 × J$1,600 = J$80,000. Direct cost = 150,000 + 20,000 + 80,000 = J$250,000. Leaving out labour gives J$170,000.

questions.q: What price should Kadeem quote, before any GCT?
questions.why: Overheads: 250,000 × 1.2 = J$300,000. Profit: 300,000 × 1.1 = J$330,000. Adding 30% to the direct cost in one go gives J$325,000, which is wrong because the profit is worked on the cost including overheads.

questions.q: Should Kadeem add GCT to Mrs Ebanks' quotation?
o: Yes, at the current rate, as every quotation must show GCT
Yes, but only on the materials part of the total price
No, because steel staircases are not subject to GCT
No, as only a business registered for GCT may charge it
questions.why: Only a business registered for GCT may charge it. Kadeem must watch his sales and register once they pass the set level; then he adds GCT at the current rate.

questions.q: What is the profit as a percentage of the selling price (the margin)?
o: About 9.1%
About 24.2%
questions.why: Profit is 330,000 − 300,000 = J$30,000, and 30,000 ÷ 330,000 × 100 = about 9.1%. The 10% is the mark-up on cost, not the margin on price.

questions.q: In Garfield's cash flow forecast, what is the closing balance at the end of month 1?
questions.why: Opening J$500,000 + cash in J$0 − cash out (1,100,000 + 300,000) = −J$900,000. He must arrange a deposit, stage payments or finance before he starts.

questions.q: Once Garfield invoices the hotel, what is the money the hotel owes him called?
o: Creditors
Overheads
Debtors
Equity
questions.why: Customers who owe the business money are debtors (accounts receivable). Suppliers the business owes are creditors.

questions.q: Which way of paying for the MIG set lets him use it now, spread the payments and own it at the end?
o: Leasing
Hire purchase
Paying from savings
An overdraft
questions.why: Hire purchase spreads the cost and the machine becomes his at the end, usually at a higher total cost. With a lease he may never own it; savings and the overdraft are needed for the cash gap.

questions.q: Which niche do Trudy-Ann's findings support best?
o: Gates and grilles, like the three shops nearby
Stainless railing work for hotels and villas
Imported railings bought in and resold at a mark-up
General repairs for anybody who happens to call
questions.why: Nine of twelve managers wait weeks for work from Kingston, she has the right qualification, and no local rival offers it: a real gap that matches her skills.

questions.q: Which further research would best test whether the niche can pay?
o: Ask the managers what they pay now and how often
Count all the hotels between Negril and Black River
Ask her family and friends whether they like the idea
Find out how many welders in Kingston use TIG
questions.why: Knowing what customers pay now and how often they need work tells her whether there is steady demand at a fair price. Kind friends and simple counts do not.

questions.q: Which unique selling point fits her research best?
o: The lowest prices of any welding shop in Westmoreland
A shop open seven days a week all through the year
A wide range of gate and grille designs on show
Stainless repairs done locally within one week
questions.why: Her customers' problem is the 4–6 week wait. A clear, checkable promise to fix that sets her apart; competing on lowest price or gates puts her against shops that already do it.

questions.q: How many tank stands a month would Orville need to sell to break even on tank stands alone?
questions.why: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution = 192,000 ÷ 24,000 = 8 tank stands a month. Using the J$18,000 profit figure instead of the contribution gives the wrong answer of about 11.

questions.q: Which change to his strategy do Orville's records support best?
o: Stop making tank stands and concentrate on the gates
Push tank-stand sales harder and look again at gate prices
Raise every price by the same amount across the board
Keep things as they are, as both kinds of job make a profit
questions.why: A tank stand makes three times the profit of a gate, so it is worth marketing harder, for example to farmers and hardware stores. The thin profit on gates suggests checking how they are priced and made.

questions.q: What should Orville do about the missed hiring milestone in his review?
o: Find why it slipped, then set a new date or step
Hire someone at once so that the plan is back on schedule
Drop the goal, as plans never work out in the real world
Leave it out of the review, as only money measures count
questions.why: A review compares results with the plan, finds the reason for any gap (perhaps cash, or not enough steady work) and records a new date or a changed step, so the strategy stays a working plan.

questions.q: A credit union asks for collateral before it will lend. What does this mean?
o: An asset the lender may take if the loan is not repaid
A fee paid to the credit union for arranging the loan
Proof that the business is registered with the tax office
A person who will run the business if the owner is sick
questions.why: Collateral, or security, is something of value such as a vehicle or land title. It lowers the lender's risk, but the owner can lose it if repayments stop.

questions.q: A customer offers to pay cash for a gate "with no receipt", so the sale is not recorded. What should the owner do?
o: Agree, but only for small jobs that are paid in cash
Agree, and give a small discount for the cash payment
Give a proper receipt and record the sale as normal
Record the sale later if the shop has a slow month
questions.why: Every sale is recorded and receipted. Hiding sales breaks tax law, makes the records useless for planning, and weakens the business's case with a lender.

questions.q: A shop owner's first employee starts next week. What must the owner do about the employee's pay?
o: Pay the helper in cash and keep no records, as he is new
Make the statutory deductions and pay them over on time
Leave the helper to sort out his own tax and NIS payments
Wait until the first year is over before registering as an employer
questions.why: An employer registers, deducts income tax, NIS, NHT and education tax from wages, adds the employer's contributions, and pays them over on time, with written terms and payroll records.
